rationale: The industry-adjusted term is essentially the net external financing / composite issuance anomaly (Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan, Daniel-Titman) and the positive-OCF indicator retains ~three-quarters of firms while dumping all loss firms at exactly zero in the middle of the cross-section, so it adds a mass-point artifact rather than genuine conditioning.

This is the well-documented net equity issuance anomaly with a profitability tilt, and the product of two same-signed ranks is internally muddled — the low end of the signal pools low-profitability firms (predicting low returns) with net repurchasers (predicting high returns), so the expected negative sign only holds at the top of the distribution.

Net debt retirement scaled by assets is the known debt-financing/leverage-change anomaly, and the rank-product suffers the same directional inconsistency as its equity twin (bottom decile mixes unprofitable firms with net debt issuers), making it a cosmetic sibling of the previous proposal rather than a distinct mechanism.

oancf/dvt is undefined or explosive for the majority of firms with zero or trivial dividends so coverage and stability are badly compromised even after winsorizing, and what survives is close to a standard payout-yield-times-quality composite whose low end conflates non-payers with poorly covered payers.

Negated share-count growth is a direct restatement of the Pontiff-Woodgate share issuance anomaly, and the positive-earnings indicator merely zeroes out loss firms, creating a large artificial point mass rather than a real interaction.

The first-difference of net external financing is a genuinely less-trodden variant of the financing anomaly and the regime-transition story is coherent, though the test should check that the signal is not simply proxying last year's issuance level (which itself predicts low returns and could flip the sign) and should address the zero mass-point created by the profitability indicator.
